title: Python Essentials for AI Developers
summary: Set up a modern Python environment and master the core patterns—virtual environments, typing, async I/O, and structured data handling—that you'll rely on in every LLM-powered project.
objectives: Set up an isolated Python project environment with virtual environments and dependency management
Use type hints and Pydantic models to validate and structure LLM inputs and outputs
Write async functions to make concurrent API calls efficiently
Handle JSON and structured data cleanly when working with LLM responses
Apply error handling and retry patterns for unreliable network calls

quiz.q: Why should you use a virtual environment for each Python project?
options: To isolate dependencies so they don't collide between projects
To automatically encrypt your API keys
quiz.why: Virtual environments isolate each project's dependencies, preventing version conflicts between projects.

quiz.q: What is the primary benefit of using Pydantic with LLM output?
options: It validates and coerces text into typed Python objects, catching malformed data
It replaces the need for try/except
It stores your API keys securely
quiz.why: Pydantic validates LLM output against a defined schema, coercing it into typed objects and raising clear errors on bad data.

quiz.q: Why is async particularly well-suited for LLM API calls?
options: LLM calls are CPU-bound and need multiple cores
LLM calls are I/O-bound, so concurrency reduces total waiting time
Async makes the model more accurate
quiz.why: LLM calls spend most time waiting on the network (I/O-bound), so running them concurrently with asyncio dramatically cuts total wait time.

quiz.q: Which function runs multiple coroutines concurrently and waits for all of them?
quiz.why: asyncio.gather schedules multiple coroutines to run concurrently and returns when all have completed.

quiz.q: What technique is used to space out retries after failed network calls, and what is its name?
quiz.why: Exponential backoff waits progressively longer (e.g., 2**attempt seconds) between retries to avoid hammering a failing service.

quiz.q: Which dict method safely returns a default when a key may be missing from LLM output?
quiz.why: dict.get(key, default) returns the default instead of raising a KeyError when the key is absent, which is common with unpredictable LLM responses.

resources.label: Python venv and virtual environments guide

body_markdown:
## Why Python for AI Developers

Python is the lingua franca of AI. Nearly every LLM provider ships a Python SDK first, and the ecosystem (Pydantic, httpx, asyncio, FastAPI) is built around the patterns you'll use to ship real apps. This lesson focuses on the practical subset of Python you actually need—not the whole language.

## Setting Up Your Environment

Never install packages globally. Each project gets its own isolated environment so dependencies don't collide.

```bash
# Create and activate a virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

# Install dependencies
pip install openai pydantic httpx python-dotenv

# Freeze for reproducibility
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

Store secrets like API keys in a `.env` file (never commit it) and load them with `python-dotenv`:

```python
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()
api_key = os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]
```

## Type Hints: Your First Line of Defense

Type hints make code self-documenting and let editors catch bugs before runtime. They're essential when passing structured data to and from LLMs.

```python
from typing import Optional

def summarize(text: str, max_words: int = 100) -> str:
    ...

def find_user(user_id: int) -> Optional[dict]:
    ...
```

## Pydantic: Validate LLM Output

LLMs return text—often JSON-shaped text that may be malformed. Pydantic models validate and coerce that data into typed Python objects, raising clear errors when something is wrong.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Recipe(BaseModel):
    title: str
    servings: int
    ingredients: list[str]

# Parse model output safely
raw = '{"title": "Soup", "servings": 4, "ingredients": ["water", "salt"]}'
recipe = Recipe.model_validate_json(raw)
print(recipe.servings)  # 4, as an int
```

Many modern LLM SDKs accept a Pydantic model directly to enforce structured outputs.

## Async: Talk to APIs Concurrently

LLM calls are I/O-bound—you spend most time waiting on the network. `asyncio` lets you fire many requests concurrently instead of one at a time, dramatically speeding up batch work.

```python
import asyncio
import httpx

async def fetch(client: httpx.AsyncClient, prompt: str) -> str:
    resp = await client.post("https://api.example.com/v1/chat",
                             json={"prompt": prompt})
    return resp.json()["text"]

async def main(prompts: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        tasks = [fetch(client, p) for p in prompts]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

results = asyncio.run(main(["hi", "hello", "hey"]))
```

Key rules: use `async def` to define coroutines, `await` to call them, and `asyncio.gather` to run many concurrently. Never block an event loop with synchronous sleeps or heavy CPU work.

## Handling JSON and Structured Data

You'll constantly convert between JSON and Python objects. The `json` module handles the basics; Pydantic handles validation.

```python
import json

data = json.loads('{"key": "value"}')   # str -> dict
text = json.dumps(data)                  # dict -> str
```

Use `dict.get(key, default)` to avoid `KeyError` when a field might be missing—common with LLM output.

## Error Handling and Retries

Network calls fail. Wrap API calls in try/except and retry transient errors with backoff.

```python
import asyncio

async def call_with_retry(fn, retries: int = 3):
    for attempt in range(retries):
        try:
            return await fn()
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == retries - 1:
                raise
            await asyncio.sleep(2 ** attempt)  # exponential backoff
```

## Putting It Together

A typical AI app flow: load config from `.env`, define Pydantic models for your data, make async calls to the LLM, validate the response, and handle errors gracefully. Master these patterns and the rest of the course will feel natural.

slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll cover the practical Python patterns you'll use in every LLM-powered project: setting up your environment, type hints, Pydantic validation, async programming, and clean data handling. We're focusing only on what you actually need to ship AI apps.

slides.title: Why These Python Skills Matter
bullets: Every major LLM provider ships a Python SDK
The ecosystem is built on typing, async, and Pydantic
Focus on the practical subset, not the whole language
These patterns repeat in every project you'll build
slides.narration: Python is the default language of AI development. Almost every provider ships a Python SDK first, and the surrounding tools like Pydantic, httpx, and asyncio shape how you write code. Rather than teaching all of Python, we focus on the handful of patterns you'll use over and over.

slides.title: Set Up an Isolated Environment
bullets: Create a virtual environment per project
Activate it before installing anything
Freeze dependencies for reproducibility
Store secrets in .env, never in code
slides.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install openai pydantic httpx python-dotenv
pip freeze > requirements.txt
slides.narration: Always isolate each project in its own virtual environment so dependencies never collide. Activate it, install your packages, and freeze them to a requirements file for reproducibility. Keep secrets like API keys out of your code—store them in a dot-env file that you never commit, and load them at runtime.

slides.title: Type Hints
bullets: Make code self-documenting
Let editors catch bugs before runtime
Essential for structured LLM data
Use Optional, list, dict annotations
slides.code:
def summarize(text: str, max_words: int = 100) -> str:
    ...
slides.narration: Type hints describe what your functions expect and return. They make code self-documenting and let your editor flag mistakes before you ever run the program. This matters even more when you're passing structured data in and out of language models.

slides.title: Pydantic: Validate LLM Output
bullets: LLMs return text that may be malformed
Pydantic coerces JSON into typed objects
Raises clear errors on bad data
Many SDKs accept models for structured output
slides.code:
class Recipe(BaseModel):
    title: str
    servings: int
    ingredients: list[str]

recipe = Recipe.model_validate_json(raw)
slides.narration: Language models return text—often JSON-shaped, sometimes malformed. Pydantic models let you validate and coerce that text into typed Python objects, raising clear errors when a field is missing or the wrong type. Modern SDKs can even take a Pydantic model directly to enforce structured outputs.

slides.title: Async: Concurrent API Calls
bullets: LLM calls are I/O-bound—mostly waiting
async lets you run many requests at once
Use async def, await, and asyncio.gather
Never block the event loop with heavy work
slides.code:
async def main(prompts):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        tasks = [fetch(client, p) for p in prompts]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
slides.narration: LLM calls spend most of their time waiting on the network. With asyncio you can fire many requests concurrently instead of one at a time, which dramatically speeds up batch processing. Define coroutines with async def, call them with await, and run many together with asyncio.gather. Just don't block the event loop with synchronous sleeps or heavy CPU work.

slides.title: JSON and Structured Data
bullets: json.loads turns strings into dicts
json.dumps turns dicts into strings
Use dict.get(key, default) for missing fields
Combine with Pydantic for validation
slides.code:
import json
data = json.loads('{"key": "value"}')
value = data.get("missing", "fallback")
slides.narration: You'll constantly move between JSON and Python objects. The json module handles the basics with loads and dumps. When a field might be missing—common with LLM output—use dict.get with a default to avoid crashes. For anything more complex, reach for Pydantic to validate the shape.

slides.title: Error Handling and Retries
bullets: Network calls fail—plan for it
Wrap API calls in try/except
Retry transient errors with backoff
Re-raise after exhausting retries
slides.narration: Network calls fail regularly, so build resilience in from the start. Wrap calls in try-except, and retry transient failures using exponential backoff—waiting longer after each attempt. If you exhaust your retries, re-raise the error so it surfaces clearly rather than failing silently.
